slides.title: High-Level Concurrency with `concurrent.futures`
slides.prompt: The `concurrent.futures` module provides a clean high-level interface for asynchronously executing calls using pools of threads or processes (`ThreadPoolExecutor` and `ProcessPoolExecutor`), returning `Future` objects.
slides.codeSnippet:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import time

def task(n):
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return n * 2

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(task, i) for i in range(5)]
    for future in as_completed(futures):
        print(future.result())

slides.title: Choosing Between Executors
options: When tasks are primary I/O-bound (network requests, disk operations)
When tasks require heavy compute operations on 16 CPU cores
When complete process memory isolation is strictly required
When bypassing the CPython GIL is mandatory
slides.correctAnswer: When tasks are primary I/O-bound (network requests, disk operations)

slides.title: Purpose of as_completed()
slides.prompt: What is the primary benefit of iterating over futures using `concurrent.futures.as_completed()`?
options: Yields futures immediately as they finish execution, regardless of submission order
Forces all tasks to execute sequentially in array index order
Automatically retries failed futures up to 3 times
Cancels remaining queued tasks if one fails with an exception
slides.correctAnswer: Yields futures immediately as they finish execution, regardless of submission order

slides.title: Canceling Futures
slides.prompt: Under what condition will calling `future.cancel()` return `True`?
options: If the task is currently sitting in the work queue and has not yet started running
Even if the task has already finished executing completely
Only if the task is currently running in an active thread
Future objects cannot be cancelled once submitted
slides.correctAnswer: If the task is currently sitting in the work queue and has not yet started running
